# Ref_Estate Playbook

When I land on an unowned property early in the game (laps 1-3), I will buy it if I have the cash, since properties generate ongoing income and contribute to my final score.

When I calculate my current balance, I will track: last declared balance + salary from passing START + all transfers received this turn, minus any rent or purchases made, and I will verify this arithmetic carefully before declaring my new balance.

When I'm considering a property purchase, I will check whether my available cash covers the purchase price. If it doesn't, I will decline and hold my cash rather than over-committing.

When I pass START, I will remember to add my salary (25) to my balance calculation for that turn.

When I land on a property I own, I will declare [pay: none] since no rent is due to anyone.

When I land on an opponent's property, I will calculate the rent owed, verify I have sufficient funds, and pay it. I will not attempt to avoid payment.

When I'm on the final lap (lap 6), I will not buy properties since there's no time for them to generate value for my score.

When settling a turn, I will always respond with all three required tokens in the exact format specified, making sure my final declared balance reflects all payments and receipts for that turn.

I will buy properties selectively in laps 1-3, focusing on affordable properties (50-100) that offer reasonable rent-to-cost ratios, rather than attempting to buy every unowned property I land on. Expensive properties like Exchange (120) may not be worth the cash outlay early on.

I will track not just my own deeds and cash, but also note which opponents own which properties and what rents I owe them, so I can anticipate future payment obligations when I land on their properties.

My score is calculated as my final declared cash plus the purchase price of all deeds I hold. Buying one property (Quarry for 60) early generated ongoing rent income from opponents and contributed meaningfully to my final score. I should aim to own 2-3 properties by the end of lap 3 to maximize score potential.

When I receive rent payments from opponents, I will add them to my balance on the turn they are credited by the bank, not on the turn I landed on their property.

I should not be too conservative with property purchases in laps 1-3; holding excessive cash without owning income-generating properties is a missed opportunity, since rent income compounds as the game progresses and more opponents land on my properties.

# Playbook for ref_estate

When I land on an unowned property, I need to decide whether to buy based on my cash position and strategic value. Early acquisitions (laps 1-3) are critical because they build deed portfolio value, which is essential for final scoring. I should buy properties when I have cash available, keeping only a minimal reserve (20-30) for immediate rent payments. Waiting too long to buy leaves me cash-rich but deed-poor at the end.

When I land on START and collect salary, I add that to my balance before declaring it.

When I land on an owned property, I pay the rent due to that investor and subtract it from my balance.

When I pass START during a lap (not just land on it), I still collect salary and add it to my balance.

I must track my cash carefully after each transaction and declare my new balance accurately. I did this correctly throughout, so continue this practice.

My core problem in this episode: I bought only two properties (Foundry for 100, Depot for 50) early, but then failed to acquire more in the mid-game when I had the opportunity. In lap 2, I had 148 cash and declined to buy Exchange for 120—a critical mistake. In lap 3, I had access to other properties but did not purchase. By lap 5, it was too late and I couldn't afford Terrace at 70. I ended with 65 in cash and only 150 in deeds for a final score of 215, while opponents who bought more properties scored higher.

When deciding whether to buy: if a property costs less than my current cash minus a small reserve (50), I should buy it in laps 1-3. Properties costing up to 120 are acquisition targets in early laps because the deed value compounds over remaining laps. In lap 2, I should have bought Exchange (120) even at 128 cash because holding it for 4 remaining laps generates income and adds deed value. Do not be cautious about large purchases early—the game rewards aggressive acquisition.

By lap 4-5, if I haven't acquired enough properties, it's nearly too late. At this point, only buy if I have very clear cash for it (no tight margins). The critical window is laps 1-3.

Once I have properties, my final score is balance plus deed values, not just balance. This means I should prioritize accumulating properties over hoarding cash. A property held for multiple laps (generating incoming rent and increasing portfolio value) beats sitting on cash that gets drained by outgoing rent payments.

Incoming rent is your friend: when other investors land on my properties and pay me, that cash should immediately be available for buying new properties on my next turn. Track incoming payments carefully and plan to deploy that cash into new acquisitions.

When I have very low cash (under 20), I cannot afford to pay rent and must prioritize collecting salary at START. Plan routes to pass START more frequently if I'm in this position.

Investor behavior: watch what other investors buy early. If they're acquiring properties aggressively, I need to match their pace or I'll fall behind in deed portfolio value and lose on final scoring even if my cash balance is higher.

Recalculate my final score: I need to know my deed portfolio value. After each purchase, track which properties I own and their purchase prices. At the end, this deed value plus my cash balance is my score.

# Playbook for ref_estate

**On property purchases:**

When I encounter an unowned property, I calculate whether buying it leaves me with enough cash cushion to survive landing on opponents' properties without going broke. A property that costs 80+ and leaves me with less than 25 cash creates dangerous exposure over remaining laps. I will not buy properties that reduce my liquidity below a safe threshold relative to the highest rents still in play.

When I have adequate cash and the property is low-to-mid value with solid rent (like 50-70 with 10-20 rent), I buy it early. Cheap properties like Depot (50, rent 10) generate consistent income throughout the game and don't cripple my liquidity. The scoring system rewards deed ownership plus cash, so owning properties is essential—but only if I can afford the risk.

I should avoid buying expensive properties (80+) in laps 3 and beyond. My experience shows that buying Exchange for 120 on lap 3 left me with only 42 cash by lap 4, starving me of liquidity when I needed it most. By lap 3, focus shifts to preservation: hold my current deed portfolio, pay rents without complaint, and let opponents overextend themselves. Expensive purchases in mid-game are traps.

On the final lap (lap 6), I should not buy properties at all. By lap 6, the game is nearly over, and purchasing properties leaves me with lower declared cash on the final count. My priority on lap 6 is maximizing my cash balance, not acquiring new deeds. Cash on the final turn is more valuable than one additional property deed.

**On rent payments:**

When I land on an opponent's property and owe rent, I pay it immediately and accurately. I track my remaining balance precisely so I know my liquidity status going forward. Rent payments in mid-game are unavoidable costs; I plan for them by maintaining adequate cash reserves.

**On passing START:**

I track whether I've passed START this turn or not. When I do pass START, I gain 25 cash—this is income I must account for and can enable purchases I couldn't otherwise afford. Passing START on lap 4+ is worth less strategically since I have fewer laps left to generate additional income, but every 25 cash matters when cash reserves are tight.

**On mid-game strategy (laps 3-5):**

By lap 3, I should shift from acquisition to preservation. If I own 1-2 cheap properties (Depot, Quarry), that's enough; hold cash and wait. By lap 4, I should maintain 60+ cash. By lap 5, I should maintain 50+ cash. Expect to pay rent throughout mid-game, but plan to receive rental income only if I own cheap, high-traffic properties. Never let aggressive early buying strand me with less than 50 cash by lap 5.

The experience of this game shows that conservative play works: I started lap 4 with 96 cash and received modest income and rent payments, ending lap 6 with 117 cash and one deed (Depot, 50). Final score 167. This is a solid position. If I had bought more aggressively, I would have likely ended with lower total cash and a worse score.

**On the final lap (lap 6):**

On lap 6, my only goal is to maximize declared cash plus current deeds. Do not buy anything. Do not take any action that reduces my final cash declaration. If I have 100+ cash on lap 6, that's a winning position; anything below 50 cash signals I played too aggressively in mid-game.

**General strategy going forward:**

Buy 1-2 cheap properties (50 or less) in laps 1-2 while I have cash, then shift to preservation mode. Aim to maintain 60+ cash by lap 4 and 50+ cash by lap 6. By lap 3, stop buying expensive properties entirely. The final score is deeds plus cash—but cash matters far more if I'm liquidity-constrained. Never let aggressive early buying strand me with <50 cash by lap 5. Cheap property ownership + high cash reserves beats expensive property ownership + low cash reserves.
